_readme: Content for page IV. Edit text here, not in iv.js. Every evidence item needs sourceIds that exist in 'sources'. Ratings are team judgments (1-5, higher = more promising; for risk, higher = lower risk). Pitch-length edit: about 2-3 evidence items per slide; numbers shown in a chart are not repeated in text. Open checks before presenting: confirm Stanford SNT's regulatory status; company revenue figures stay hidden until verified against filings; confirm the timeline dates listed in charts.stimulationTimeline.dateNotes.

thesis.headline: Brain stimulation has the most promise, and the other two fields will reach patients through it.

sentences.text: Stimulation is the only one of the three that is already improving patients' lives, backed by independent randomized trials and an adaptive system approved in 2025.
Connectomics will help decide where to stimulate, and biohybrid implants may one day replace the electrode that does it.
The bottleneck now is getting working devices to patients: picking who should get one, programming it, referring people to it and getting it paid for. That is where new companies can win.

framework.intro: We used six criteria, each taken from a tool that funders, regulators or investors already use to judge medical technology.

criteria.name: Magnitude of the problem and potential impact
questions: How big is the problem, and how much better could this be?
criteria.lookedFor: How many people are affected, and where current care falls short.

criteria.name: Scientific evidence and technical maturity
questions: Does it reliably work, ideally in humans?
criteria.lookedFor: Studies and trials that have been repeated.

criteria.name: Translation and time to impact
criteria.test: How soon could it reach patients?
questions: What blocks real use, and for how long?
criteria.lookedFor: What is still unsolved, and the regulatory route.

criteria.name: Customer demand and adoption
questions: Who needs it, who pays, and why switch?
criteria.lookedFor: Whether people adopt it, who pays, and why they would switch.

criteria.name: Commercial viability and scalability
criteria.test: Can this become a sustainable business?
questions: Can it become a scalable business?
criteria.lookedFor: Market size, costs, insurance coverage and competitors.

criteria.name: Risk, uncertainty, and responsible deployment
questions: What could break the thesis or harm people?

ratingScale.direction: Higher is always better. For risk (criterion 6), a higher rating means less risk.
ratingScale.note: These ratings are our team's judgment, not measurements.

biodesignNote.text: Following Stanford Biodesign's guidance, we rated only what is known today, not what might happen.

levels.label: Strong
levels.meaning: Repeated evidence in people and a clear path forward.

levels.label: Good
levels.meaning: Solid evidence, with gaps that look manageable.

levels.label: Mixed
levels.meaning: Real evidence, but major questions are still open.

lenses.name: Patients
lenses.rationale: Benefit, evidence, speed and safety count most.

lenses.name: Founders
lenses.rationale: Demand and whether it can become a business count most.

lenses.name: Science
lenses.rationale: Scientific impact and the quality of the evidence count most.

framework.lensNote: There is no single right way to weight the criteria, so you can choose whose priorities to use.
framework.lensSummary: Equal counts every criterion the same, Patients puts benefit, evidence, speed and safety first, Founders puts demand and business potential first, and Science puts scientific impact and the quality of the evidence first.
framework.trlFootnote: Our estimate on the US Department of Defense's readiness scale for medical technology, not an official rating.

c1.rationale: The needs are severe, but the benefit in the brain is still a projection.

c2.rationale: It works in the arm, but brain data exists only in rodents.

c3.rationale: Key problems are unsolved, and use in the human brain is 10 or more years away.

c4.rationale: The need is urgent, but no one has tested demand for a brain device.

c5.rationale: It is expensive, the regulation is unclear and payment would be slow.

c6.rationale: Living, modified cells bring unknown immune risks.

c1.rationale: Its impact could be broad, but only through other products.

c2.rationale: Fly maps make accurate predictions, but mammal maps are tiny samples.

c3.rationale: A whole mouse brain is 10 to 15 years away.

c4.rationale: The buyers are researchers and funders.

c5.rationale: The data is open, which makes it hard to build a business on.

c6.rationale: There is little risk to patients, but noisy maps can mislead.

c1.rationale: The need is large and growing, and it beats drugs in trials.

c2.rationale: Several independent randomized trials, some of them blinded.

c3.rationale: It is in clinics now, but programming the devices is still hard.

c4.rationale: The benefit is clear, but few eligible patients are referred.

c5.rationale: Insurers already pay for it, and the opening is in personalizing it.

c6.rationale: Surgery carries risk, some trials did no better than placebo, and access is unequal.

fields.name: Human brain stimulation
fields.verdict: Already helping patients. The next gains are in personalizing it and getting it to more people.
fields.definition: Electrical or magnetic energy that changes brain activity. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) uses implanted electrodes, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) uses a coil held against the head. Adaptive DBS adjusts itself in real time.

slides.verdict: The need is large and growing, and stimulation already does better than drugs.

evidence.text: Parkinson's cases may more than double by 2050, to 25.2 million.
In the EARLYSTIM trial, quality of life rose 26% with stimulation and fell 1% on drugs alone.
Stanford's five-day SNT treatment for depression beat placebo stimulation (50% versus 20.8% in remission), although the effect faded over 12 weeks.

slides.verdict: By far the most mature of the three, with one warning.

evidence.text: Randomized trials favored DBS over the best medication. In the VA trial, the hours a day with good symptom control rose from 6.4 to 10.9.

evidence.qualifier: Many trials at high risk of bias
evidence.text: A 2026 meta-analysis of 30 randomized comparisons found strong, high-certainty antidepressant effects for TMS.

readiness.label: Conventional DBS for Parkinson's
readiness.note: Independent randomized trials, including double-blind ones.

readiness.label: Stanford SNT
readiness.note: Two placebo-controlled randomized trials at one site.

readiness.label: DBS for depression
readiness.note: Two pivotal trials were stopped early.

caveats: Several key trials were funded by industry.

slides.verdict: In clinics now. What is left is precision and programming.

evidence.text: Programming adaptive DBS is not fully worked out yet, and in one clinic only 9 of the 20 patients offered it qualified.
UCSF is testing an automated way to recommend adaptive DBS settings, so clinics without specialists can use it.

caveats: Timelines for psychiatric DBS depend on the TRANSCEND trial.

slides.verdict: Patients who get it keep it, but most never get it.

evidence.text: 98% of ADAPT-PD participants chose to remain on adaptive DBS.
Only about 10% of eligible Parkinson's patients are referred for it, partly because many doctors don't realize how safe DBS is.

caveats: Most adoption data comes from Parkinson's.

slides.verdict: Insurers already pay for it, and the opening is software that personalizes the programming.

evidence.text: Most insurers cover DBS for Parkinson's, and adaptive DBS runs on sensing devices that are already in use.
DBS needs skilled clinicians to program it, and the devices now record data that could help automate that.

We built a piece of that software: a small neural network that predicts the brain's mu rhythm from scalp EEG, so a TMS pulse can land on the wave's trough, the timing linked to stronger effects. The full write-up is linked in the sources.

Tested on 9 people it never trained on, it put 71% of simulated pulses on target with a 40 ms system delay, against 53% for the standard method and 25% for untimed TMS. It beat both published methods for all 9 people.
With a 60 ms delay it was as accurate as the standard method with no delay at all, so cheaper hardware could deliver timed TMS. A few minutes of each person's own EEG improved it for all 9.
One study found that mu phase made no difference to how strongly TMS excites the motor cortex, so the benefit of timing still has to be shown in patients.

caveats: The software opening is our own inference.
Our demo used recorded EEG, not live stimulation.

slides.verdict: Surgery carries real risk, and access is unequal.

evidence.text: In the VA trial, 49 DBS patients had serious adverse events against 15 on medication, including one death.
Women and racial and ethnic minorities are less likely to receive DBS, even at equal severity.

caveats: Most safety data comes from experienced centers.

fields.name: Connectomics
fields.verdict: Fully mapped in a fly, but only a cubic millimeter of a mammal brain so far.
fields.definition: Maps of how neurons connect, from every synapse in tiny tissue samples to MRI maps of the major fiber tracts. It is a research tool, so it helps patients only through what gets built on top of it.

overviewReadiness.label: Whole maps of small brains (worm, fly)

slides.verdict: Possibly the biggest problem of the three, but it helps patients only indirectly.

evidence.text: Conditions of the nervous system were the top cause of lost healthy life in 2021, affecting about 3.4 billion people.
A simulation built only from fly wiring correctly predicted which neurons sense taste and start feeding.

slides.verdict: Fly maps hold up and make predictions. Mammal maps are tiny samples that are only partly checked.

evidence.text: Two independent fly maps agreed on most cell types and strong connections, but about a third of previously proposed cell types could not be found again.
Tracing about 1,500 mouse neurons took years and over a million manual fixes.

readiness.label: Whole maps of small brains (worm, fly)
MRI connectomes for clinical prediction
readiness.note: Validated in groups of DBS patients.

readiness.label: Whole mouse brain
readiness.note: Not done yet; methods are at pilot scale.

slides.verdict: A whole mouse brain is 10 to 15 years away. For a whole human brain, we found no credible timeline.

evidence.text: Wellcome's expert group set a whole mouse connectome as a 10 to 15 year goal, and proofreading alone might take about 100,000 person-years with today's methods.
E11 Bio's protein barcodes let AI trace neurons on cheaper microscopes, and the company predicts a mouse map in about five years.

slides.verdict: The buyers are researchers and funders. Demand from clinics comes through stimulation.

evidence.text: NIH's BRAIN CONNECTS program is building pipelines to map whole mammalian brains.
Demand grows as maps get cheaper, and E11 Bio claims a route to 100 times lower cost.

caveats: Desk research only; we haven't interviewed buyers yet.

slides.verdict: Weak as a business by design, because the data is free and open.

evidence.text: The flagship datasets (MICrONS, FlyWire, E11 Bio) are released free and open.
Only a few centers could image a whole mouse brain, but the later software steps could be done anywhere.

slides.verdict: Little direct risk to patients, but noisy maps can mislead.

evidence.text: MRI tractography produces more invalid fiber bundles than valid ones, which is dangerous if maps guide treatment.
Wiring maps leave out neuromodulators, the chemicals that change how circuits behave.

caveats: Low direct risk is our judgment, since mapping uses tissue outside the body.

fields.name: Biohybrid implants
fields.verdict: Working in people's arms, but still only a promise for the brain.
fields.definition: Electronics paired with living cells, so the body meets biology instead of bare metal. Examples are a muscle graft that amplifies a cut nerve in the arm, or engineered neurons that wire into the brain.

slides.verdict: The biggest claimed upside of the three, but the benefits for the brain are projections.

evidence.text: Nearly 5.4 million Americans live with paralysis and nearly 2 million with limb loss.
Science Corp claims orders of magnitude more bandwidth than current implants, but an outside expert says its device isn't yet an interface on its own.

slides.verdict: Works in the arm. In the brain there is one rodent study, and signals only flowed one way.

evidence.text: A 2026 meta-analysis of 238 patients found no painful nerve growths (neuromas) after RPNI surgery, against 20 of 99 with standard care.
In mice, Science Corp's grafted neurons connected, but the change in behavior wasn't statistically significant and signals flowed only one way.

readiness.label: RPNI for pain prevention (biological only, no electronics)
readiness.note: Cohorts at several centers; no randomized trials.

readiness.label: RPNI with implanted electrodes for prosthetic control
Science Corp stem-cell biohybrid
readiness.note: Mouse preprint; signals one way only.

caveats: An RPNI on its own is purely biological. It becomes biohybrid once electrodes are added.

slides.verdict: A human brain device is likely a decade or more away.

evidence.text: Developers need a universal cell line that hides from the immune system, because grafts made for each patient would cost over $1 million each.
No one has shown a two-way biohybrid interface yet, and Science Corp's first human device is a sensor without living cells.

slides.verdict: The need is real, but no one has tested demand for a brain biohybrid.

evidence.text: Many adults stop using their prostheses: average rejection rates were 26% for body-powered and 23% for electric ones.
Investors are paying now: Science Corp raised a $230 million Series C at a reported $1.5 billion valuation.

caveats: We haven't interviewed patients yet, and funding shows belief, not demand.

slides.verdict: Cost, regulation and slow payment make the business speculative today.

evidence.text: No company has worked out the regulatory route for a device that contains living neurons.
Small device makers had a 19.4% chance of Medicare coverage within five years, against 67.9% for large ones.
Science Corp is hedging by selling electronics and tools to other BCI companies.

slides.verdict: Living, gene-modified cells add new unknowns on top of the usual implant risks.

evidence.text: The graft has to avoid the immune system, and the long-term design uses gene-modified neurons that respond to light.
Laws on neural-data privacy are new. Colorado and California passed the first state laws in 2024.

convergence.heading: How the three fields fit together

explanation.text: Connectivity maps already predict which DBS placements help, and they guide where Stanford's SNT treatment is aimed.
Closed-loop devices stimulate only when they detect a symptom's signature in brain activity, so better decoding means better-timed stimulation.
Our TMS analysis shows the gain from timing: predicting the motor rhythm 40 ms ahead put 71% of simulated pulses on target, against 53% with the standard method.
Biohybrids aim to reach more neurons with less damage, but they are still only in animals.

alsoAnswers.heading: What this says about questions I and II

items.title: Scaling up versus a new kind of interface
items.body: Both approaches make sense, but they pay off over different time scales. Scaling up metal electrodes, as Neuralink does, builds on real use in people but has to fight the scarring that weakens signals over time. Living-neuron interfaces, like Science Corp's, could avoid that problem but have no human data yet.

items.title: What holds neurotech back
items.body: Beyond the science, three things hold it back: proving a device works better than a placebo version of the procedure, getting paid for it (a median 5.7-year wait for Medicare coverage, longer for small companies), and getting patients referred (only about 10% of eligible Parkinson's patients are). Optogenetics has reached only one patient, in the eye. If regulation changes, our evidence says it should start with payment, which is what CMS's proposed RAPID pathway targets.

connectomeScale.title: How much brain has been mapped
connectomeScale.summary: Worm and fly brains are fully mapped; mammalian maps are cubic-millimeter samples; whole mouse and human brains are unmapped.
connectomeScale.takeaway: Fully mapped in a fly, but only a cubic millimeter of a mammal brain.
connectomeScale.countNote: Counts are as reported; some studies count all cells and some only neurons.

points.label: Whole mouse brain
points.scope: About 1,000 times the data of the human sample

annotation.text: A whole mouse brain needs about 1,000 times the data of the 1.4-petabyte human sample.

connectomeScale.renderingNote: The whole mouse point has no reported neuron count in our sources; render it as a hollow dashed marker positioned between the human sample and whole human brain with the label only, and do not invent a number.

biohybridEvidence.title: Where biohybrid evidence stands
biohybridEvidence.summary: Used in human surgery to prevent pain, tested in small human studies for prosthetic control, and only in animals in the brain.
biohybridEvidence.takeaway: Working in people's arms, but only in animals in the brain.

steps.label: Brain biohybrid in humans
steps.detail: Not tried yet; the first human device will be a sensor without cells.

steps.label: RPNI with electrodes for prosthetic control

stimulationTimeline.title: Two evidence tracks in brain stimulation
stimulationTimeline.summary: Parkinson's DBS: positive trials from 2006 to 2020, and adaptive DBS approved in 2025. Depression: two DBS trials stopped, a positive SNT trial in 2022, and TRANSCEND started in 2025.

events.label: RECLAIM (DBS): stopped early because it wasn't working

stimulationTimeline.dateNotes: RECLAIM's report year (2015) comes from the Cleveland Clinic summary of its Biological Psychiatry publication; BROADEN's publication year (2017) comes from Medscape. Verify exact dates if the team wants month-level precision. INTREPID is placed at 2020, the year of the Lancet Neurology exchange about its results; confirm the primary publication year.

coverageGap.title: FDA approval doesn't mean insurers pay
coverageGap.summary: 44% of 64 novel FDA-authorized devices reached any Medicare coverage, after a median 5.7 years; small makers fared far worse.
